en: Lord Kṛṣṇa is the Supreme Controller, whose form is eternal existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Govinda is without beginning, the origin of all, and the cause of all causes.
Obeisances to Śrī Śrī Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa!
He who is equal to Sanātana, whose elder brother was the illustrious Sanātana,
and whose younger brother was Śrī Vallabha— he is that Śrī Rūpa, the supreme refuge of all living beings.
May the majesty of the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa be magnified within my heart,
by whose grace I desire to expound the Brahma-saṃhitā.
Even if difficult to reconcile, the Smṛti of the Sages is consistent with reason when properly investigated;
however, should a conflict arise here upon investigation, the Sages themselves shall be my final authority.
Although that Saṃhitā consists of one hundred chapters, nevertheless,
this chapter, by virtue of its form as a sūtra, has attained the status of being its entire limb.
That which has been perceived by those of refined intellect in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata and other scriptures is precisely what has been examined here; therefore, my mind is filled with joy.
Whatever has been established in detail in the *Śrīkṛṣṇasandarbha*,
that I shall touch upon here once more for the sake of explaining it.

Now, that which is stated in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam— namely, "These are but portions and plenary expansions of the Supreme Person, while Kṛṣṇa is the Lord Himself" (BhP 1.3.28)— is first expressed here by the word "Īśvara.
In this context, the term "Kṛṣṇa" alone is used.
The specific name itself [is used] as the qualificand,
as in "the festival of the incarnation of Kṛṣṇa" and so forth, due to its renown among great persons such as Śrī Śuka.
In passages such as "To Kṛṣṇa, to Vāsudeva, to the son of Devakī," and in the Sāmopaniṣad,
[the term is used] because it is the first to be perceived.

This undertaking concerns that mantra which was first indicated by Garga through the manifestation of its class of names (*nāma-varga*), because it is familiar from the outset and constitutes the fundamental form (*mūla-rūpa*).
As it is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*, in the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, in the dialogue between Nārada and Kuśadhvaja:
In the words of the Blessed Lord: "O scorcher of foes, the name called Kṛṣṇa is the most principal of My names.
For this very reason, in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, within the hymn of the one hundred and eight names of Śrī Kṛṣṇa:
Whatever fruit is obtained by reciting three times the thousand auspicious names,
a single name of Kṛṣṇa bestows that very same fruit in a single recitation.

Thus, although it was stated here simply as "of Śrī-Kṛṣṇa," the fact that He will later be praised by the name Govinda is indeed for the purpose of showing His specific distinction as the Lord of Cows (Gavendra) even while being Kṛṣṇa. Therefore, because of His primacy through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), He is described with such epithets as "the Lord" (*Īśvara*) and so forth. Now—
That [Supreme Being] is also perceived through his qualities,
as Garga said: "There were indeed three forms of him, assuming bodies according to the ages."
White, red, and likewise yellow, it has now turned black.
"There are many names and forms of your son, corresponding to his qualities and actions; I know them, but other people do not.
This is the meaning of these two verses.

Of this one who is seen as Kṛṣṇa, who assumes various incarnations (tanūḥ) in every age and is manifest, there were three [forms] beginning with Śukla that became manifest; and each of those [incarnations] beginning with Śukla is now, at this time of his incarnation, [present] directly from this limb of Kṛṣṇa’s. In this [context]:
Thus [the Lord] is included within this very [category].

For this very reason, because He is the agent (kartṛ) and because He is the most excellent of all, "Kṛṣṇa" is His primary name. Therefore, he says "many" to indicate that these forms belong to Him alone.
Thus, when the primacy of the name "Kṛṣṇa" has been established by way of its qualities, [it is said]:
"The word *kṛṣi* denotes the earth (*bhū*), and *ṇa* denotes bliss (*nirvṛti*)."
The supreme Brahman, which is the unity of those two, is designated as Kṛṣṇa.
Thus, its being of such a nature is obtained through its function as *yoga*.

Nor is this verse intended for anything else; for it is found in the *Gautamīya-tantra*, which is dependent upon the worship of that [deity], specifically in the commentary on the eighteen-syllable mantra. This is so.
A similar verse is seen:
"The word *kṛṣi* has the meaning of existence (*sattā*), and *ṇa* has the nature of bliss;
therefore, the Self would be of the nature of happiness because it consists of the bliss of being. Thus.

Therefore, this is the meaning: *bhū* is that from which all things (*artha*) arise; it is called the "meaning of the root" (*dhātvartha*), just like the word *bhāva*. And here, that [meaning] is specifically the meaning of the root *kṛṣ* (to draw forth), because that alone is what is attained. Even though in the *Gautamīya* (the *Nyāyasūtra*) the word *bhū* denotes existence (*sattā*), it is the very existence that is the meaning of that root which is being expressed. [For example, in the case of] "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*).
When "existence" (sattā) is expressed, only the existence of a jar (ghaṭa-sattā) is understood, and not the existence of a cloth (paṭa-sattā), nor the existence of a universal (sāmānya-sattā).
Now, cessation is bliss; their identity, manifested through grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), is that which is supreme.
Brahman is that reality which nourishes (*bṛṃhaṇa*) everything from every side; it is the greatest (*bṛhattama*) and is designated as Kṛṣṇa.

However, because the root *kṛṣ* has the meaning of "attracting" alone, and because the suffix *-ṇa* cannot be placed in grammatical apposition with the bliss (*ānanda*) to be expressed [as the result], [the name Kṛṣṇa applies] due to the relationship between the cause and that which possesses the cause.

A metaphorical identification (abhedopacāra) should be made; and that is for the purpose of indicating abundance, as in the expression "ghee [is] life. Furthermore, the word *brahman* has those respective meanings because of its vastness (*bṛhattva*) and its nourishing nature (*bṛṃhaṇatva*); therefore, it is *brahman*.
This is known from the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "They know him as the Supreme" (ViP 1.12.57).
It is stated exactly thus in the Bṛhad-Gautamīya:
"The word *kṛṣi* has the meaning of existence (*sattā*), and *ṇa* is of the nature of bliss (*ānanda*)."
"Because of the conjunction of existence (sattā) and bliss (ānanda), consciousness is called the Supreme Brahman.

Thus, even by the proponents of non-duality (advayavādins), the identity of existence and bliss must be understood in that way; for according to the Grammarians (śābdikas), they are perceived as having distinct referents.
And here, by the word "being" (sattā), that which is the supreme cause of the manifestation of all existing things is indeed denoted; for it is said:
"In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone."
Thus says the Śruti (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1).
Even if they have the same denotation, there can be no relationship of qualifier and qualified— as in the case of "tree" and "taru"— and because one would be redundant.
The verse from the *Gautamīya-tantra* should also be explained as follows:
in the first half [of the verse], Kṛṣṇa is Ānanda, characterized by the power of attracting all things.

The meaning is as follows: because, as stated in the second half [of the verse], he is thus of the nature of bliss that attracts all, therefore the self (*ātman*) and the living being (*jīva*) must be of the nature of bliss therein;
and in this regard, love (*prema*) serves as the cause.
"Because He consists of that bliss.
Thus, it should be understood that Kṛṣṇa— the one denoted by the word "Kṛṣṇa"— is the supreme, most expansive Bliss who attracts all, by virtue of both His essential nature and His qualities.
And that word is conventionally established as referring specifically to Śrī Devakīnandana.
His quality of being the source of all bliss is seen in the Vāsudevopaniṣad: "Devakīnandana gladdens everything."

And indeed, the authors of the *Nāmakaumudī* have said: "The word *kṛṣṇa* has its conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) as the Supreme Brahman, the suckling of Śrī Yaśodā, whose luster is dark like the *tamāla* tree. Therefore, this word must not be applied elsewhere.
As Bhaṭṭa has said:
"An established usage (rūḍhi), having attained its own nature, becomes a displacer of etymological derivation (yoga);
however, that which is merely to be postulated does not attain its own nature because it is sublated by etymological derivation."
Thus, His state as the Supreme Brahman is described in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam: "The Supreme Brahman, who is hidden, possesses human characteristics" (BhP 7.15.58);
He is that friend who is supreme bliss and the perfect Brahman.
"Sanātana" (the eternal), as stated in BhP 10.14.32;
and in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "Wherein the Supreme Brahman, named Kṛṣṇa, has descended in human form" (ViP 4.11.2).
And in the Śrī Gītā it is said: "For I am the foundation of Brahman" (Gītā 14.27).
And in the Śrī Gopāla-tāpanī Upaniṣad: "He who is that Supreme Brahman..."
"Gopāla," he said.
Now, let us follow the root [of the word]:
because he is precisely that which is denoted by the word "Kṛṣṇa," therefore...
Īśvara is the controller of all;
this very point has been indicated in the *Bṛhadgautamīya* by means of another meaning for the word "Kṛṣṇa" itself.

Alternatively, "The Blessed One draws forth the entire world, both stationary and moving, by means of his form as Time; therefore he is called Kṛṣṇa. The meaning of the word *kāla* is that which "measures" (*kalayati*) or restrains everything.
And likewise, in the Third Canto, with reference to Him,
Uddhava attained a definitive conclusion that He alone is complete;
yet He Himself, the Lord of the three worlds, is beyond all comparison and excellence.
"Having attained all desires through the splendor of sovereign self-rule,
his footstool is honored by the tips of the crowns of the guardians of the worlds, who have long been bringing him tribute. [BhP 3.2.21] Thus it is said.

In the Śrī-Gītā it is said: "Pervading this entire universe with but a single fraction of Myself, I remain as the world" (Gītā 10.42). In the Śrī-Gopāla-Tāpanī it is said: "Kṛṣṇa is the one, the self-controlled, the all-pervading, the worshipful" (GTU 1.19). Since He is indeed such a Lord, [He is the cause].
Therefore, he is the Supreme (*paramaḥ*):
that in whom reside all the most excellent powers (*mā*) in the form of *lakṣmī*. As it is said in the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*: "He, flooded with His own desires, took delight with the *ramās*."

Thus: "This is not the grace of Śrī, O limb, for she is ever devoted to Him" (BhP 10.47.60), and so forth; and "There the Blessed One, the son of Devakī, shone exceedingly with them" (BhP 10.33.6); "The Blessed Lord Acyuta was surrounded by those whose sorrows had been dispelled."
And it is said: "He shone forth exceedingly" (BhP 10.32.20).

Furthermore, it will be stated later in this very same work: "The beloved of Śrī is the Supreme Person" (BrahmaS 5.56). And in the Tāpanīya Upaniṣad: "Kṛṣṇa is indeed the supreme deity" (GTU 1.3). For this very reason...
He is the Supreme and, for that reason, the Origin.
As it is said in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, Tenth Canto: "Hearing that Jarāsandha was invincible, Hari meditated upon the king..."
"Indeed, today Uddhava spoke that very same means (upāya) which [Hari] spoke [in the past]," thus [it is said].
And the commentary of Svāmi-pāda states: "The first [Hari] is Śrī Kṛṣṇa";
however, in the eleventh [book], it refers to Him.
He states both his preeminence and his primacy simultaneously:
"I bow to the primordial Person, the Bull, known by the name Kṛṣṇa."

And this "primordiality" (āditva) does not depend on its entry [into manifestation], but rather it is beginningless (*anādi*), meaning that which has no beginning (*ādi*). And in the *Tāpanīya Upaniṣad*, after stating, "The one controller, all-pervading, Kṛṣṇa, the worshipful," it says, "the eternal among eternals. Because he is the beginning in such a manner, he is therefore the cause of all causes.

And likewise, in the tenth book, Devakī spoke these words to Him: "O Soul of the Universe, I have indeed gone for refuge to You, by whose fractional portion of a fractional portion the creation, dissolution, and emergence of the universe occur" (BhP 10.85.31).
And the commentary says: Of that [Prakṛti], Puruṣa is a part; of that [Puruṣa], Māyā is a part; of that [Māyā], the Guṇas are parts.
Through a portion of these—a mere atom, a tiny fragment—the creation of the universe and so forth come to be. To You, that very one...
"I have gone for refuge to the Goal"—thus it is said. And likewise, in the *Brahma-stuti*: "O dear one, Nārāyaṇa, because he is the abode of men, waters, and light" (BhP 10.14.3).
The wise know that the principles born from Nara are called "Nārāḥ";
since he was their first abode (ayana), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
The meaning is that Nārāyaṇa, who is characterized by this [etymology], is your limb (aṅga), while you are his possessor of limbs (aṅgin).
As stated in the Śrī-Gītā: "Pervading all this, I stand as the world with but one part. Thus, the etymological meaning of the word *kṛṣṇa* has also been established.

And those who, by that word, express only supreme bliss as being beyond the two [pleasures] of agriculture and women—they too, through such qualifiers as "the Lord" (īśvara) and so forth, would consider Him to possess an inherent power;
they would not consider Him to possess the power of another entity, because He is non-dual and the cause of all. Not in Him...
Because it is impossible to superimpose the power of another entity upon that which is secondless and the cause of all, so says the Śruti: "Bliss is Brahman.
For who indeed could breathe, or who could live, were it not for this Ākāśa?
There would be no bliss;
from bliss, indeed, all beings are born.
Of that, neither effect nor instrument exists.
"Neither an equal nor a superior to Him is seen;
His power is heard to be truly manifold,
consisting of innate knowledge, strength, and action" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.8).

[Objection: But surely, according to your own system and in the *Yogavṛtti*, since Kṛṣṇa is designated as the supreme, greatest bliss that attracts all, it is understood that he is indeed formless, because no form of bliss is perceived.
[Reply: True; however, this is the supreme, unprecedented form of bliss established from before.
The meaning is that His form is of the very nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*).
Thus it is said in the *Śrī Daśama-skandha* in the hymn of praise by Brahmā: "In You alone, whose body is eternal bliss and consciousness.
And likewise in the *Tāpanī* and *Hayaśīrṣa* Upaniṣads: "To Kṛṣṇa, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss, the performer of effortless deeds."

And in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*, within the *Śrī-Kṛṣṇāṣṭottara-śata-nāma-stotra*, it is said: "He who brings joy to the people of Nanda’s Vraja, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*).
This is what is meant.

Indeed, *sattva* is said to be non-deviation (*avyabhicāritva*), and its nature as such is described in the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*, Tenth Canto, in the speech of Brahmā and others: "Kṛṣṇa is established in truth; truth is established in Him."
"Govinda is truth from truth; therefore, he is indeed 'Satya' by name. Thus it is said in the words of Śrī Devakī:
"When the world has perished at the end of two *parārdhas*..."
When the great elements have returned to their primordial state,
and the manifest has passed into the unmanifest by the force of time, you alone remain, free from all designations.
A mortal, terrified by the serpent of death, fled through all the worlds but found no fearlessness today; yet,
having reached Your lotus feet by chance, he has now attained it.
"He lies at ease; death departs from him" (BhP 10.3.24), and so forth.
Furthermore, in the words of Śrī Brahmā, "You are one, the first" (BhP 10.14.18), and so forth, it is taught that "that immeasurable, non-dual Brahman remains."
In the Śrī Gītā it is said: "For I am the foundation of Brahman," and,
"Since I transcend the perishable and am superior even to the imperishable,
therefore I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as Puruṣottama (the Supreme Person)."
In the *Tāpanīya*:
"This one who stands in the sun, this one who stands among the cows—he is distinct from birth and old age; he is immovable and indivisible."
He who protects the cows,
he who dwells among the cowherds— Death fears Govinda.
And so forth.
In that context, regarding the previous passage "in Saurya": *saurī* refers to the Yamunā; the meaning is "in Vṛndāvana, which is in a location not far from that."
Now, the nature of consciousness consists in self-luminosity, as opposed to being illuminated by another;
and this has been stated by Brahmā in the *Śrī-daśama* in passages such as "You alone are the one Self," beginning with "self-effulgent" (*svayaṃ-jyotiḥ*). Also in the *Tāpanīya*:
To Him who ordained Brahmā in the beginning, and who protects the sciences for him— that Kṛṣṇa,
the Divine, who illumines the intellect of the self— [I seek refuge].
"One who desires liberation should indeed seek refuge. Thus it is said.
One does not see His form with the eye;
He is obtained only by whomsoever He chooses.
For him, this Self chooses its own body.
This is like other scriptural passages (*śruty-antara*).

Just as the nature of bliss (*ānanda-svarūpatva*) consists in being the object of supreme, unconditional love in its entirety, so too is it stated at the end of the *brahma-stava* in the *Śrī-daśama*: "O Brahman, in Kṛṣṇa, who is born from the Supreme... (*BhP 10.14.49*).
This is clear from such questions and answers;
likewise, it was experienced by Ānakadundubhi:
"You are known to me as the manifest Supreme Person, beyond primordial nature."
"His essential nature is the bliss of absolute experience, the witness of all cognitions" (BhP 10.3.13).
This is like another Vedic scripture which states, "Bliss is the form of Brahman.
Thus, it is established that His form consists of the embodiment of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānandavigraha*).
It is established that the body is indeed the self, and likewise, the self is indeed the body; therefore, it is also not the case that he lacks embodiedness, just like a living being.
This has been established as the final conclusion,
as stated by the venerable Śuka: "Know this Kṛṣṇa to be the Self of all selves."

"He too appears here as if possessing a body through *māyā*, for the welfare of the world" (BhP 10.14.55). Nevertheless, the meaning is that he acts like one possessing a body solely because he is subject to the compassion of his divine play (*līlā*). *Māyā* [is used here] in the sense of guile.
And [the word] *kṛpā* [is used] in this sense, according to the *Viśvaprakāśa*.
Thus, when it is established that His form is Śrī Kṛṣṇa with such-and-such characteristics, and because He is intent upon both types of divine play (*līlā*), in some instances...
In some places, his status as the Lord of the Vṛṣṇis and his nature as Govinda are seen.
Thus Śrī Sūta said in the twelfth [skandha]:
"O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, O friend of Kṛṣṇa, O bull among the Vṛṣṇis, O protector of the earth, O destroyer of the wicked..."
"O Govinda, whose prowess is inexhaustible in consuming the lineage of kings, whose holy fame is sung by the cowherd women and the multitude of servants,
and whose name is auspicious to hear— protect Your servants! [BhP 12.11.25] Thus it is said.
Thus, even in this way, by virtue of being distinguished by His own desired form, pastimes, and retinue, the name "Govinda" establishes that He alone is to be worshipped as one's own chosen deity;
as will be praised further on in this very same work.
"In the dwellings adorned with clusters of wish-fulfilling gems, he is the Kalpa-tree";
thus Govinda spoke at the conclusion of the consecration. Having said this, there follows the prayer of Śrī Śuka at the commencement of that section.
"May Indra be dear to us through cows" (BhP 10.26.25); for since cows are the support of all things, the status of Indra over all is established precisely by his being the Indra of cows.
Nor should this be considered inferior; thus it is said:

For it is said in the *Go-sūkta*: "From cows the sacrifices proceed; from cows the gods have arisen; by means of cows the Vedas were uttered, along with their six limbs, word-for-word recitation, and sequential arrangement."

Let it be that these cows, descended from the supreme Goloka, possess the status of queens; moreover, in the *Tāpanīya-śruti*, Brahmā himself has revealed his own worship of them: [he worships] Govinda, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss, who sits perpetually beneath the trees of Vṛndāvana.
"I, together with the hosts of Maruts, shall please him" (GTU 1.37).
Likewise, in the tenth [canto]: "That abundant fortune, this extraordinary birth in the forest... (BhP 10.14.34), and so forth; and the prayer to obtain him specifically as the joy of Śrī Nanda.
"I bow to You, the worshipful one, whose body is like a cloud and whose garment is lightning," and so forth, ending with "to the son of the cowherd woman" (BhP 10.14.1).
Thus,
by that very [passage], the word *govinda* has another meaning as well, consisting of various supreme sovereignties.

This is not accepted; and so it has been stated in the *Gautamīya-tantra*, in the explanation of the meaning of the venerable ten-syllable mantra, where the conclusion of the intended purport follows the restatement of the state of being the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) regarding the nature of Īśvara:

One should know that "gopī" refers to *prakṛti* (primordial nature) and "jana" refers to the collection of principles (*tattva*). The Lord is their support by virtue of pervading them and being their cause;
He is described as the beloved, the supreme light of intense bliss.
Alternatively, the gopīs are *prakṛti* (nature) and the people are the circle of her portions;
the beloved of these two is declared to be the Lord known as Kṛṣṇa, the Sovereign.
Therefore, He is celebrated by the Vedas as the Lord of both cause and effect.
"Or rather, He is the very husband of the gopīs who have attained perfection through many births;
He is called the Delight of Nanda, the increaser of the joy of the three worlds.
Thus [it is said]. "Prakṛti" means that which is called Māyā, the causal power of the universe; this refers to the aggregate of the principles (tattvas).
The form consisting of Mahat and the rest is the substratum of these two; it is the supreme light of intense bliss, the Lord,
who is designated by the word "Vallabha."
The cause of lordship is both by way of pervasion and by way of causality.
"Prakṛti" means the power known as Mahālakṣmī, who is his own essential nature (*svarūpa*), who transcends *māyā*, and who manifests in Vaikuṇṭha and other realms. This is the meaning.
The "portion-circle" (*aṃśa-maṇḍala*) refers to forms such as Saṅkarṣaṇa and others.
Regarding the phrase "of those perfected through many births," [it is said]:
"Many births of mine have passed, as well as yours, O Arjuna."
Thus, according to the words of the Śrī Bhagavad-gītā (4.5), the purport is precisely that there is an beginningless succession of births;
therefore, even here, the status of being the son of Nanda is intended, as was stated by Śrī Garga.
"Previously, this son of yours was born somewhere as Vāsudeva. For his status as a "son" (ātmaja) is intended to mean precisely that he manifested within the mind of Śrī Vasudeva as well.
"He entered with a portion of His part into the mind of Ānakadundubhi" (BhP 10.2.16).
Likewise, He established within Śrī Devakī His own self, which is the Self of all, just as the ultimate limit (kāṣṭhā) produces bliss from the mind.
From such passages as this, and because the result was likewise for Śrī Vrajeśvarī,
the cause is inferred from the result; namely,
the manifestation of the Blessed Lord.
Because it is seen everywhere, pervading all times immediately preceding [the manifestation],
yet even when that [manifestation] occurs within the self, it is only the pure, great love consisting of the state of being a father that leads to the status of being one's own child.
This is the motive:
because even when the Lord Varāha manifested from the presence of Brahmā, there was no such perception of mutual existence between them.
Likewise, Lord Nṛsiṃha was born from two pillars;
nor should it be said that sonship would only exist upon entering the womb.
Furthermore, when [the Lord] entered the womb of His mother for the sake of protecting Parīkṣit, such behavior did not exist between them; therefore,
the very love designated as *vātsalya* (parental affection) is the cause of being a son.

Such pure love, however, belongs only to the two Lords of Vraja; for Śrī Vasudeva and Devakī, the knowledge of supreme sovereignty was an obstacle—thus it was rightly said previously: "This [love] belongs to Vasudeva."

Then Śrī Śukadeva likewise concluded: "This son of the Gopikā, the Blessed One, who is the auspiciousness of all the worlds, is not easily attained by embodied beings" (BhP 10.9.21). This was also determined by those learned in the Āgamas.
"Nanda-gopa's son is a deity.
Therefore, even in the application of the glorious ten-syllable mantra, he is seen as being composed of that very essence.
Now, as for the specific details, they should be seen in the *Śrī-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*, beginning with the verse: "Then Nanda was born as His son" (*BhP* 10.5.1).
The great abode called Gokula is a thousand-petaled lotus.
That is its pericarp, that is its abode, and it arises from its infinite portions.
Now, he establishes its eternal abode as the proof of its possessing that very nature, beginning with the words "the thousand-petaled lotus.
That lotus is one in which there are thousands of petals. It is the ground.
"Consisting of a multitude of wish-fulfilling gems" refers, according to what will be stated later, to a lotus made of wish-fulfilling gems;
that is the great, most excellent *pada*, meaning the supreme abode of the Great Śrī-Kṛṣṇa.

The meaning is that the "foot" (pada) of the Great Blessed One refers to Mahāvaikuṇṭha and so forth; for, according to the maxim that "conventional usage supersedes etymological derivation," that very [meaning] is what is understood. With this in mind, it was said in the Śrī Daśama:

We desire to go, we long to attain—that is, we yearn for them. What are they distinguished by?
They are those in which there are cows with many horns, meaning great-horned cows, or alternatively, those possessing many auspicious marks.

"Ayāsaḥ" means "auspicious. According to the *Amara-kośa*, "ayaḥ" signifies "that which brings auspiciousness," and this is a word ending in the nominative plural (*jas*), just like "devāsaḥ. In this context:

It is well known in the world and in the Veda that the supreme abode of the lotus feet of the Lord Himself, the wide-striding one (Urugāya)— known as Śrī Goloka— shines forth profusely and in manifold ways; thus he says, "the Veda [declares it]."

In the Yajurvedic texts, the Mādhyandina recension is praised in passages such as "We desire the abodes" (*dhāmāny uśmasi*). Here, they read another variant: "The supreme step of Viṣṇu shines forth" (*viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam avabhāti*) and "the vast one" (*bhūri*);
the rest is the same. //5//

Thus, for that god who consists of light, who is beyond the highest and eternally blissful, there is by his very nature no association with the material world (prakṛti), as he delights in the Self alone.
Now, let us follow the root commentary (*mūla-vyākhyā*).

Just as the state of being a single Puruṣa is described in the *Puruṣasūkta* and other texts by intending to express the non-difference between Virāṭ and His inner controller (*antaryāmin*), so too [is it here].
He speaks thus regarding both Goloka and its presiding deity: "The Lord" (devaḥ) refers to Goloka,
and its presiding deity is in the form of Śrī Govinda.
"Ever-blissful" (sadānanda) means its very nature; its neuter gender is according to the Vedic revelation: "Consciousness, bliss is Brahman.
[This refers to] one who delights in the Self.
There is no contact with *māyā* by nature for that which is independent of anything else;
as it is said in the Second Canto: "Where there is no *māyā*, much less others who are devoted to Hari, in whom gods and demons alike pay homage" (BhP 2.9.10). //6//
For one who sports with Māyā, there is no separation from her; he delighted in his own Self through Rāmā, having abandoned all time due to the desire to create. // BrS_5.11 //
That goddess Niyati is Ramā; she is dear to Him, and at that time she was under His control.

Now, he says "by Māyā" to show that the Puruṣa, who is a portion of that [Prakṛti] whose nature is phenomenal proliferation (prapañca), does not possess such a quality; for even during the dissolution of Prakṛti, He remains as its locus (ālaya), as indicated by such passages as "by means of a portion of a portion of a portion."
[Objection: "In that case, would He not be non-supreme (anīśvara) because of being smeared by that [world], just like the individual soul (jīva)? To this he says: "By the Self" (ātmanā).
But He, indeed, rejoiced—attained delight—by means of the Self through His internal function, namely, by Rati, which is His own essential power (svarūpa-śakti), and not externally.
The meaning is that he is to be served through such illusory power (māyā).

This bestower of boons upon those who have taken refuge, having assumed incarnations characterized by the [three] qualities, shall delight [the world] with his own power as he performs whatever he intends to do.
This is because of the hymn to Brahman in the third canto [BhP 3.9.23],

and because of the words of the venerable Arjuna in the first canto: "Having cast off māyā by means of the power of consciousness (cic-śakti), he abides in the Self in the state of absolute isolation (kaivalya)" [BhP 1.7.23].
To the question, "In that case, how can there be creation without His impulsion?

he replies: From the delight (ramaṇa) by which He took pleasure in such a manner—having abandoned [Himself] through the desire to create (sisṛkṣayā), that is, the wish to emanate, and having dispatched Time (kāla) for the purpose of creation.

The reading with the nominative case-ending (*prathamānta-pāṭha*), however, is easy to understand; the sense is that she is accomplished by that very [power] in the form of its majesty (*prabhāva*). As it is said: "They call power *pauruṣa* (manly vigor), while others say time is the source of fear" (BhP 3.26.16).
But by the operation of time, the powerful Adhokṣaja infused his seed into Māyā, who consists of the guṇas, through the Puruṣa who is his own self.
And thus from the third [skandha]: "But who is that very *rati*? To this he says with half a verse: "It is *niyati*," for she is herself that which is regulated.

The fact that eternality resides in the Blessed One alone is *niyati*, which is her power (*śakti*) as her very own nature (*svarūpa*). The term *devī* means "the shining one," whose form is self-luminous; this is the meaning. As it is said in the twelfth [chapter]: "She is the non-departing one (*anapāyinī*)."
"The Blessed Śrī is the manifest self of Hari" (BhP 12.11.20). And the commentary states:
"She is the non-departing power (*śakti*) of Hari.
The reason for this is 'the manifest self,' meaning [she is the self] of his essential nature (*svarūpa*)."
The meaning is that because she is of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), there is no difference between her and that [consciousness]. This is the point.
Here, by the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) and by the statement beginning with "by whom she, being ashamed, was unable to stand within the path of vision," it is implied that *māyā* is not present.
In that regard, her imperishability is as stated in the *Viṣṇu-purāṇa*:
"O best of the twice-born, that Śrī, the mother of the world, is eternal and inseparable from Viṣṇu; just as Viṣṇu is omnipresent, so too is she. [ViP 1.8.17]
And thus it is said: "Just as Janārdana, the Lord of the World, the God of gods, takes an incarnation, so too does Śrī act as his companion. And:
"In the state of divinity she possesses a divine body, and in the state of humanity she is human."
"He indeed makes for himself a body from the form of Hari's own body" (ViP 1.9.145).
And in the *Hayaśīrṣa-pañcarātra*: "The Goddess is not without Viṣṇu, nor is Hari without the Lotus-born.
(7) The eternal Lord Śambhu, in the form of light, is his *liṅga*.
That which is the womb is the supreme Śakti; Kāma is the seed of the Great Hari.
Now, it may be objected that the causality of Śiva and Śakti is heard of nowhere;
in that case, [the author] states "that linga" as a specific limb [of the system], [explaining that] it is a conceptual construction like the description of the Virāṭ.

According to the *Viṣṇu-purāṇa*, "this power of the universe resides within a ten-millionth part of a ten-millionth part of him"— referring to that Great Blessed One who is the self of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), whose form is unmanifest because it is veiled by the light of his own partial manifestations.
The *liṅga* of the Puruṣa is that very portion which, acting as the locus of the *liṅga*, produces the phenomenal world;
he alone is Śambhu. The meaning is that any other [manifestation] is called Śambhu only because it is a particular manifestation (*āvirbhāva-viśeṣa*) of him.
And it will be stated: "Just as milk is produced [as curd] through its connection with a specific transformation into curd, but not [independently] from that [milk itself]."
"Distinct from the cause," and so forth.

Likewise, that which is the source—the womb-like constituent—of that illusion (*māyā*), which consists of the application of effort and the form [of the world] yet remains unmanifest, is itself the other power called *pradhāna*, as previously described. In that regard:
And for that Hari, who is the portion of Hari known as Puruṣa, desire arises for the sake of creation; the meaning is that the wish to create (didiṛkṣā) is born.
And from that, "the Great" (mahat) arises, which is the nature of the Mahat-tattva together with the individual soul (jīva).
And from the third [sūtra], *tu māyāyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.85):
"These subjects belonging to Maheśvara are born with the nature of both the male organ and the womb."
In reality, however, it is precisely the state of being the prior intention; thus he says with the half-verse beginning "liṅga": "māheśvarīḥ" means "belonging to Maheśvara. // 9 //
This powerful Puruṣa is Maheśvara in the form of the Liṅga;
within that Liṅga, Mahāviṣṇu, the Lord of the world, manifested.

Having restated that very point with the half-verse beginning "the possessor of power" (*śaktimān*), he states with the half-verse beginning "in that" (*tasmin*) that there is once again the manifestation, in a manifest form, of that previously mentioned unmanifest form within it. Therefore,
even that portion which is the producer of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) in the form of the *liṅga* is called the "powerful person" (*śaktimān puruṣa*).

He is also called Maheśvara; therefore, when that *liṅga* had reached the state of being composed of the subtle elements (*bhūta-sūkṣma*), Mahāviṣṇu himself, who is the possessor of its parts, appeared—manifesting in a visible form. For he alone is the Lord of all worlds, both high and low, and of all living beings. (10)
The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet;
he has a thousand arms, is the self of the universe, possesses a thousand rays, and is the progenitor of a thousand.
He explains that very form with the words "thousand-headed":
he whose thousand parts are incarnations is the "thousand-parted" one (*sahasrāṃśa*).
He who procreates or creates a thousand is "Sahasra-sūḥ";
the word *sahasra* here refers to everywhere to incalculability.
And this is another form of that very same [word].
It has been stated: "The first incarnation of the Supreme is Puruṣa" (BhP 2.6.42).
Regarding this, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says:
"The first incarnation of the Supreme, the Infinite One, is that playful form described in the verse beginning with 'He who has a thousand heads'. //11//
From that eternal [Lord], the Blessed Nārāyaṇa appeared as the ocean of causes, the treasure-store whose nature is Saṅkarṣaṇa; within him,
the Great One himself, possessing a thousand rays, entered into yogic sleep.

He says "Nārāyaṇa" in one and a half verses [to show] that this very one is the one who lies within the causal ocean. Those waters themselves appeared as the reservoir of the causal ocean, and he is Nārāyaṇa, whose nature is Saṅkarṣaṇa. Previously, as the covering of Goloka, he was recognized as Saṅkarṣaṇa among the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha).
The meaning is that this [universe] is a portion of Him alone. As it has been said:
"The waters are called *nārāḥ*; for the waters are indeed the offspring of Nara (*nara-sūnavaḥ*).
Since they were His primary abode (*ayana*), He is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa. (12)
Within the network of the pores of his hair, the seed of Saṅkarṣaṇa produced golden eggs enveloped by the great elements.
Therefore, he describes the origin of the cosmic eggs with the words "tad roma" (his hair).
The word "tat" (that) means "of him" (tasya);
that very seed of his, who is of the nature of Saṅkarṣaṇa, which was superposed upon the power of the womb, is what existed previously.

Having reached the state of being as subtle as the ultimate atoms (*bhūta-sūkṣma*), it subsequently entered into the pores and networks of hair-follicles; having become internalized there, golden eggs were produced, which means they were produced by the great elements (*mahābhūta*) in their unquintuplicated (*apañcīkṛta*) portions.

This was stated by Brahmā in the tenth [canto]: "Where is Your greatness—[a greatness] consisting of wandering through countless cosmic eggs as subtle as atoms, and traversing the path of the winds within the pores of Your skin? (BhP 10.14.11).
And in the third [verse]:
"This outer egg-shell, accompanied by its modifications, joined with the specific elements (viśeṣa) and so forth, is fifty crores in extent."
"Wherein, having entered like an atom, one who has increased tenfold more than that is perceived, and within him there are indeed millions of other multitudes of cosmic eggs. [BhP 3.11.39–40] Thus.
"In this manner, for every single cosmic egg, He Himself enters from each respective portion. [BrS 5.18]
The thousand-headed, universal self, the eternal Great Viṣṇu.
And so, he says "in every egg" (*pratyaṇḍam*) to show that He Himself entered into those cosmic eggs individually, both in His own form and in other forms,
by means of one part after another (*ekāṃśād ekāṃśāt*).
The meaning [of the verse] is as follows: // 14 // He created Viṣṇu from his left side and Prajāpati from his right side;
he brought forth Śambhu, who consists of the *jyotir-liṅga*, from the region of his pubic hair (*kūrca*).
He states what he did next with the words "from his left side" (*vāmāṅgāt*).
These [deities], Viṣṇu and the others, are the protectors and so forth of all cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*); they correspond to the Viṣṇus and others who reside within each individual cosmic egg.

They are the agents who employ their own partial manifestations (svāṃśas). The sense is that just as it is within each individual Brahmāṇḍa, so too should it be understood throughout the entire sphere of Brahmāṇḍas.

In these [mantras], this Prajāpati is indeed in the form of Hiraṇyagarbha and not merely in the form of the four-faced one to be described hereafter; he is the creator of the various deities residing within their respective coverings (āvaraṇas).
Viṣṇu and Śambhu are also to be understood as the agents of their respective functions of preservation and withdrawal;
[the latter] from the region of the *kūrca* (the upper lip) and from between the eyebrows. Of these...
The locations should be known as being within the veil of water alone.
From that [ego], this universe, consisting of ego, was born.

In this regard, he also states another function of Śambhu with the half-verse beginning "consisting of ego" (*ahaṅkārātmakam*). This entire universe was born—that is, came into being—from that very [source] as consisting of ego.
The meaning is that the state of the universe consisting of ego arose from Him, because He is the presiding deity over all egos.
as he truly displayed his grace through those three kinds of manifestations,
the divine Yoga-nidrā was united with him, like Śrī herself.

He now describes the pastimes of Him who has entered the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) and assumed various forms, beginning with the words "atha taiḥ" (then by them). By means of those three kinds of similar forms— namely, the Viṣṇu-forms and others residing within each cosmic egg— He sustains His pastimes consisting of the protection and other functions within the cosmic egg.
"He carries her" means he carries her who belongs to the Person within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*);
that is the meaning.
"Yoga-sleep" refers to the Blessed Lady who constitutes a portion of the aforementioned Great Yoga-sleep.
Because she consists of the samādhi of the bliss of her own essential nature (*svarūpānanda*), she is like Śrī who is united with all-encompassing sovereignty that has become internalized;
the meaning is that just as Śrī is united with him even in part, so too is she. 17.
Then, from his navel, while he was desirous of creating, a lotus emerged.
That golden lotus-stalk led to the wondrous world of Brahmā.
And thus, regarding the phrase "in the desire to create":
that golden lotus, joined with its stalk (*nāla*), is not [merely] a stalk; because it serves as the locus for both the birth and the abode of Brahmā, the meaning is "the world. //18//
The principles, established from of old, are mutual causes;
yet, due to the absence of inherence and conjunction, they remain distinct and separate. (BrS 5.23)
Then the Blessed One, the Primal Person, being occupied with His own conscious power, the Lord,
employing His illusory energy, entered into yogic sleep.

Likewise, in order to explain the awakening of the collective individual soul (samaṣṭi-jīva), which consists of innumerable individual souls, he describes the process of creation according to what is stated in the Third Canto regarding the Lord reclining upon the ocean of causal matter, using the three verses beginning with "The principles" (tattvāni).

Regarding this, he says two things: "joining the principles with one another through illusion by means of his own power" means that immediately after joining them, he, being devoid of effort, entered into the very state of yogic sleep (yoga-nidrā). // 19 //
Having joined those very [limbs], he himself entered the cave;
when he had entered the cave, the individual soul (jīvātman) awakens.
Now he states the third [verse] with the words "having joined" (*yojayitvā*).
The meaning is: having joined that [mind] in the interval between *yojanā* (joining) and *yoga-nidrā* (yogic sleep). "The caves" (*guhāḥ*) refers to the body of Virāj.
He awakens; he wakes from the sleep of dissolution.
He is eternal, eternally connected [to consciousness], and that primordial nature (prakṛti) is indeed supreme.
He states the soul's natural state with the half-verse beginning with "He is eternal" (nityaḥ).

"Eternal" means existing from time without beginning or end; he is one whose inherent connection (samavāya) with the Lord is perpetual, just as the sun is [eternally connected] to its web of rays—this is the sense.
That consciousness which, though situated as a witness, has emerged from its own self-awareness and is colored by the passion for the qualities (guṇas), is called the individual soul (jīva).
Thus from the Nārada-Pañcarātra:
"In the world of living beings, my very own eternal portion exists as the individual soul."
Thus, from the Śrī-Gītā Upaniṣads as well:
for this very reason, *prakṛti* exists in its own essential nature merely as a witness,
in the form of its own reflection.
The meaning is that he has attained the state of the knower (pramātṛ), as if having reached primordial nature (prakṛti).
As it is said in the Śrī-Gītā itself: "Know my supreme prakṛti, which has become the individual soul (jīva)."
And the Śruti text, "Two birds, united, friends," reveals His eternal nature.
Thus, from the navel of Hari, there arose a lotus connected to the Self of all.
There, Brahmā came into being once more, four-faced and possessed of the four Vedas.
Now, he says "thus" (evam) to explain that the abode of the universal individual soul (*samaṣṭi-jīva*) has arisen from the Person who has entered the cave.
Then, he explains the emergence of the body of experience for that Hiraṇyagarbha-Brahmā, who identifies with the universal body, by saying "therein" (*tatra*). 22.
Born by the power of the Blessed One and impelled at that very moment, he— refined by his prior latent impressions— set his mind upon the desire to create;
he beheld only darkness everywhere and nothing else whatsoever.
Now, with the verse beginning "sa jātaḥ," [the author] describes the activity of that four-faced one; this is clear.
Then, a divine voice spoke before him:
"O Govinda! O Kṛṣṇa! O Gopī-jana! and so forth.
Your beloved will give you the mantra dear to the Fire-god, which is pleasing to him.
Then, with one and a half verses, he spoke of the grace of the Lord obtained through the fortune of his previous worship; this is clear. 24.
"You are austerity; by this austerity, your perfection shall come to pass."

This very point regarding the "contacts" (*sparśa*), namely that which is the sixteenth and the twenty-first, is applied according to the third chapter by means of the half-verse beginning with *tapas tvam*. This is clear.
Then he performed austerities for a very long time, pleasing the imperishable Govinda.
To Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śvetadvīpa, who resides in Goloka, the highest of the high.
He was attended by Prakṛti, who is embodied in the form of the qualities (guṇas),
upon a lotus endowed with a thousand petals and thickened by ten million filaments.
There, upon a great seat in the form of a *karṇikāra* flower, whose ground is a wish-fulfilling gem,
sits the eternal one, whose nature is light, consisting of consciousness and bliss.
He plays the flute composed of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman) from his lotus-like mouth,
surrounded by a host of playful women, and praised by his own various partial manifestations (aṃśas).

But he, by means of that mantra, in accordance with his own particular desire, worshipped Śrī Govinda—who is distinguished by the power of the Creator—as will be described; and according to your [the listener's] perspective, [he worshipped Him] as being present in the sacred seat (pīṭha) called Gokula. Thus he says in four verses beginning with "atha tepe" (then he performed penance).

It was attended by her who is composed of the qualities (guṇas)— that is, by her whose form consists of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas; she, being embodied and possessing a physical form, worshipped him from outside Gokula, standing there and honoring him through meditation and other such means.
"Being bashful in the presence of the Supreme," and "the blinking eyes carrying the offering along with the Unconquered One."
From the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam: "By means of His portions, which are the attendants situated within those coverings. Now follows the movement of the flute's resonance, which consists of the three Vedas.
Quivering, she quickly entered the lotus-like faces of the Self-Existent One.
Having received the Gāyatrī from him as he was chanting it, the Lotus-born One was consecrated by the primordial qualities and thereby attained the status of the twice-born.

Thus, it is said in the two verses beginning with "atha veṇu" that his status as a twice-born (*dvijatva*), like that of Dhruva, was produced by the mantra presiding over him which he worshipped, occurring only after his initiation (*dīkṣā*);
for Gāyatrī is the embodiment of the three Vedas (*trayī-mūrti*) because she is the mother of the Vedas.
And because that very [state] has become manifest in the second verse as well;
"his way" (tanmayī gatiḥ) refers to the sequence [of verses].
"He entered the lotus-faces" by means of the eight ears.
The meaning is that he entered.
By the primordial teacher, Śrī Kṛṣṇa. 27.
Then Vidhi (Brahmā), awakened by the Triple Veda, realized the ocean of reality.
He praised Keśava with this hymn, which is the essence of the Vedas.

And then, having received even the three Vedas from him, he praised him alone; thus [the author] says "by the three" (trayyā). He is Keśava because he weaves—that is, spreads out—the *keśas*, which are the rays (*aṃśu*).
"Those rays of mine which shine forth are designated as *keśas*."
Therefore, the best of sages call me Keśava, the omniscient one.
Thus, from the *Bhārata* passage cited in the *Keśava-nirukti* as raised by the commentary on the *Sahasranāma*:
"He who protects [the world] in palaces made of wish-fulfilling gems, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of *kalpa*-trees, and where the *surabhi* cow [provides all needs]..."
I worship that Govinda, the primordial person, who is served with great reverence by hundreds of thousands of Lakṣmīs.
He expresses praise with the words beginning "cintāmaṇi" and so forth.
In that regard, within this Goloka, through the differentiation of mantras,

And although there are other sacred seats (pīṭhas), he first praises [the Lord] by means of the single verse beginning with "cintāmaṇi," through the primary play of residing in the sacred seat known as Goloka, which is central to all;
that is, in every respect.
He was protecting [them] by means of leading them to the forest, bringing them back from the cow-pen, and tending to them; he was guarding them with affection.
Yet, at times, there was a sense of distinctiveness in private, as he said: "O Lakṣmī."
It has already been explained that the "splendors" (*lakṣmyaḥ*) here refer specifically to the beautiful cowherd women.
[He saw him] sounding his flute, with eyes as broad as lotus petals,
adorned with a peacock feather crest, and with a body as beautiful as a dark rain cloud.
I worship that Govinda, the primordial person, whose extraordinary beauty is more lovely than ten million Cupids.

Thus, having described the pastimes occurring in the extraordinary seat known as Goloka— consisting of wish-fulfilling gems, palaces, and the like, including narrative, song, drama, and movement— in accordance with what will be stated hereafter; [the author now describes] those pastimes situated in a single location, devoid of narrative, song, and so forth, as perceived through extensive meditation and other means.
He describes the playfulness (*līlā*) residing in the second seat with the two verses beginning "the flute" (*veṇu*).
Regarding "the flute," it is clear in that context. //30//
Adorned with a forest garland shimmering with restless moonbeams,
a flute, and jeweled armlets; the dark-complexioned one, graceful in his three-fold bend, who delights in the playful arts of love and whose radiance is eternally manifest.
I worship that Govinda, the primordial Person.
"Ālolita," and so forth:
he whose *vilāsa* (graceful charm) consists precisely in that cleverness (*vaidagdhyā*) found in playful jesting preceded by affection.
"Fluid play and jesting," according to Amara.
May he whose limbs possess the functions of all the senses,
and who beholds, protects, and sustains the worlds for a long time, [grant us grace].
I worship that Govinda, the primal Person, whose form is eternally radiant, consisting of bliss, consciousness, and existence.
Having thus described the two-fold pastimes, He speaks of the specific manifestations of His supreme, inconceivable power through four verses beginning with "The limbs.

[The word] "jaganti" means worlds.

and therein lies the distinctive excellence of that form.
Thus he states the reason, beginning with "Ānanda":
"Non-dual, infallible, without beginning, of infinite form,
the primordial, ancient Person, and yet possessed of fresh youth."
I worship that Govinda, the primordial Person, who is difficult to find in the Vedas but not difficult to find in devotion to the Self.
With these three [verses], he nourishes the very uniqueness of non-duality;
the meaning is that non-duality consists of earth, and the king is non-dual, being incomparable.
And there was the amazement of himself and of Uddhava,
who stood third, due to Uddhava's words: "For His devotees do not fall away from Acyuta even in the great calamity of universal dissolution."
Therefore, he alone is Acyuta (the Unfallen) in all the world, omnipresent and imperishable.
Thus, from the words of the *Kāśī-kāṇḍa*:
"Alas, Kaṃsa, having come today for this favor, you shall see the lotus-foot of Hari, sent by him."
Those who had previously crossed over the darkness so difficult to traverse did so by means of the radiance of the circle of his toenails once he had descended.

"That which is worshipped by the gods beginning with Brahmā and Bhava, and by Śrī," and so forth, from the words of Akrūra in the tenth chapter; "She who is indeed worshipped by Śrī, by Brahmā, and others whose desires are fulfilled."

The words of the illustrious Uddhava:

"Appointed by Him, I create; Hara, under His control, destroys;
and He who sustains the three powers protects the universe in the form of Puruṣa. [BhP 2.6.33] Thus it is said.
Just as the flame of a lamp, having reached another wick, [continues its light].
I worship that Govinda, the primordial person, who shines as Viṣṇu himself, illuminating like a lamp through the commonality of the nature of the revealed cause.
Now, describing the single form of Hari as it follows in sequence,

he defines Viṣṇu as a partial incarnation (guṇāvatāra) by way of the context of the Great Lord (Maheśa), who is also a partial incarnation; he does so with the verse beginning "dīpārciḥ," which provides the reason for his being such.
Regarding the phrase "having a manifest cause and common characteristics":
if one is a portion of a portion of Śrī Govinda who reclines upon the causal ocean, then [another] is one who reclines within the embryonic waters (garbhodaka) of that [ocean].
And although it is understood that Viṣṇu is an incarnation of him, nevertheless, he is like a very subtle and stainless lamp that has arisen from a great lamp through a succession of transmissions.
Just as there is a similarity with him in respect to the aspect of being of the nature of light,
so too is Viṣṇu understood by Govinda; but as for Śambhu—
Because it is the locus of darkness, it is not equal [to the Self], which stands in the place of the subtle flame of a lamp made of light; to make this known, it is stated thus:
"even for Mahāviṣṇu, because he is but a particular portion (kalā)."
Because it will be demonstrated [later].
He who, with every pore of his body containing infinite world-eggs, used to rest in yogic sleep upon the waters of the causal ocean;
Relying upon that supreme foundational power (ādhāra-śakti), I worship Govinda, the primordial Person, who is my own true form.
Now he describes Him who reclines upon the ocean of causes:
"He whose pores [are filled] along with the infinite cosmic eggs of the world. The absence of the prior placement of the word *saha* (along with) is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*).

[He meditates upon] his own supreme form, consisting of the power of the foundational support (ādhāra-śakti), known as Śeṣa; relying upon whose single exhalation [the world lasts for] a period of time... //47//
The lords of the cosmic eggs live by the hair-pores of that Great Viṣṇu, of whom [Brahmā] is a particular portion;
I worship that Govinda, the primordial person.

In this regard, Mahāviṣṇu— who is the protector of the entire cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) and who has been shown as your own incarnation, both by virtue of his association with Mahābrahmā and others and by virtue of being distinct from them—
is here described in such a manner, portraying him as possessing the same characteristics as that [Supreme Being].
The lords of those respective world-eggs, such as Viṣṇu and others, live and remain manifest in the world by virtue of their respective offices.
Just as the sun [manifests] its own radiance within its own fragments of stone... //48//
In the same way, even though this Brahmā, the creator of the cosmic egg of the universe, manifests his own power to some extent here,
I worship that Govinda, the primordial Person.

Thus, having shown that the Goddess and others have Him as their substratum, and showing that of Brahman as well by way of a relevant connection (*prasaṅga*), the author clarifies the very nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) as being extremely distinct [from Him] with the words "the radiant one" (*bhāsvān*). "The radiant one" (*bhāsvān*) refers to the sun.
Just as [the sun] manifests some of its own brilliance within its own stones known as *sūryakānta*, which are renowned for being eternally its own;
by the word "api" (also/even), it is implied that by means of that [brilliance].
By means of its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), it performs actions such as burning by itself;
likewise, it manifests a certain degree of light within that specific individual soul (*jīva*).

The meaning is that, by virtue of that limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), being himself Brahmā, he becomes the ordainer within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*)— the creator of the individual creation (*vyaṣṭi-sṛṣṭi*).
Or rather, this is described as Mahābrahmā himself;
and it should be understood that Mahāśiva is characterized by him.
And therefore, His being the architect of the cosmic eggs is indeed logical. Although Māyā, known as Durgā, is the servant of Him who reclines upon the causal ocean,
and although Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others are His incarnations who recline within the waters of the womb, nevertheless, for Him—
Because they are the support of all, those [elements] are also reckoned as being supported by it;
the same applies hereafter. 49.
Having placed the pair of his lotus-like feet upon the jar—
At the time of salutation during the conjunction [of the two], that Lord of the Gaṇas is fully capable of destroying the obstacles of these three worlds;
I worship Him, Govinda, the Primordial Person.

Now, one might raise the objection that since everyone first praises Gaṇapati for the sake of warding off all obstacles, he alone is worthy of praise; anticipating this, the author refutes it with the verse beginning "yat-pāda-," establishing that very point by way of a *kaimutya* (a fortiori) argument.

This was confirmed by the illustrious Kapiladeva: "By the sacred water (tīrtha) flowing from his feet—the foremost of rivers—having been placed upon his head, Śiva became truly auspicious (Śiva)" (BhP 3.28.22).
Fire, earth, ether, water, wind, and the directions...
I worship that Govinda, the primordial person, from whom time, the self, and the mind arise— these three worlds— which come into being, pass away, and enter into him.
And that is logical, as he says: "Agni is the great...
All is clear. That which is the eye of this Savitṛ among all the planets...
I worship that Govinda, the primordial Person, whose command causes the King— the embodiment of all gods and possessor of infinite splendor— to revolve, wielding the wheel of time.
Some declare the Lord of All to be accompanied by the Sun (Savitṛ), as it is said: "That which is the eye"—meaning He who is the illuminator of the eye;
"The splendor residing in the sun which illumines the entire world."
Know that radiance which is in the moon and that which is in the fire to be mine.
Thus from the Gītās:
"Out of fear of Him the wind blows; out of fear the sun rises."
This is because of such scriptural passages as these,
and because the Virāṭ-form itself possesses the eye of the Sun. 52.
Dharma, the accumulation of sins, the sacred scriptures, ascetic penances,
and all living beings from Brahmā down to the smallest insects and birds—
whose power is made manifest by the mere granting of [His] glory.
I worship that Govinda, the primordial Person.
What more need be said? Regarding the word "Dharma":
"I am the source of all; from me everything proceeds" (Gītā 10.8), according to the Śrī Gītā. 53.
But he who extends [his grace] to one who is a vessel for the fruits corresponding to the bonds of his own karma— whether that being be an Indragopa insect or Indra himself—
burns away the karmas of those who possess devotion.
I worship that Govinda, the primordial Person.

Therefore, although He is equal to all as the giver of fruits according to their respective karma—according to the maxim that "the Lord of All should be viewed like the rain-cloud"—He nevertheless shows a special partiality toward His devotee; thus he says: "But he who [is Indra]... and so forth.

"I am equal toward all beings; for me there is neither aversion nor affection. But those who worship Me with devotion, they are in Me, and I too am in them" (Gītā 9.29). Thus: "Those people who, thinking of no other, worship Me with constant meditation..."
"And for those who are constantly devoted to Me, I provide their acquisition and preservation (yoga-kṣema)," as stated in the Śrī Gītā (9.22). 54.
[And for those who are afraid of anger, desire, natural affection, and so forth...]
Through affection, delusion, reverence for the guru, and the sense of being a servant,
they contemplated and attained forms similar to his;
I worship that Govinda, the primordial Person.

He who bestows even upon his enemies a fruit difficult for others to obtain— how much more so upon those who are foremost among the desireless (niṣkāma) because their desires and the like are directed toward Him alone?
Therefore, who else is there to be worshipped?
Thus, with the words "I honor him," he concludes the section on the internal [attitudes] by saying "whom [I honor] as anger.
*Sahaja-praṇaya* is friendship; *vātsalya* is the affection appropriate for a father and so forth; *moha* is delusion.
A state consisting of the forgetting of everything;
the non-manifestation of the Supreme Brahman;
reverence for the Guru.

The meaning is as follows: "consisting of the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of one's own [teacher] as a father and so forth" refers to the contemplation that "this person is to be served by me," which is servitude (*dāsya*). "Similar to that" means similar to one who is possessed by anger through a portion of the non-material (*aprākṛta*) nature.
The meaning is that it is equal [to others] by virtue of the degree to which it attains the portions of form and qualities suitable for cultivation;
[this applies even when] one or another [factor] is unseen (*adṛṣṭa*).
"In the world, he is equal in the qualities of character and nobility"—this is the statement of Śrī Vāsudeva;
"except for the activity of maintaining the universe"—this is the Brahma-sūtra.
While I am being employed [in that task], toward her...
Furthermore, from the perspective of the statement of Śrī Nārada, "the pure body of a devotee," there is a contradiction if [the Lord] were in every respect identical to Him;
for in passages such as "by whom the kings [were slain] out of enmity," [the Lord is described as being perceived by those whose minds are devoted].

Furthermore, by asking "How so? and then answering "Because their minds were well-attached," he demonstrates the very identity of the two [forms] who have descended from the manifold expansion (prapañca) residing in Goloka. As it has been said:
"But Nanda and the others, having seen him... and so forth. (55)
The beauties are Śrī’s beloveds; the Supreme Person is her beloved; the trees are wish-fulfilling kalpa-tarūs; the ground is composed of clusters of cintāmaṇi jewels; the water is nectar;
the conversation, song, dance, and even the movement of the flute are dear friends.
That supreme light is both consciousness-bliss and that which is to be tasted.
I worship that Śvetadvīpa, which they here call Goloka, where the milk-ocean flows from the Surabhis, and where not even a moment known as half a blink of an eye passes.
Only a few virtuous ones, who move through the world at rare intervals, truly know you.

Thus, having praised his own chosen deity as one worthy of worship, he praises the world distinguished by that deity with the following pair of verses beginning with "śriyaḥ kāntāḥ. Here, "śriyaḥ" refers to those who possess the beauty of the lovely women of Vraja; it is of them alone [that he speaks].
Because he is universally established in both mantra and meditation,
even though those [women] are infinite, he alone is their beloved;
thus, his world is superior to that of Parama-Nārāyaṇa and others, as well as to their respective worlds.
The majesty has been demonstrated;
for it is well known that the trees are "wish-fulfilling trees" (kalpa-taru) because they bestow everything upon all of them.
And likewise, the earth and so forth grant all desires; how much more so the Kaustubha gem and the like?
Even water is as sweet as nectar; how much more so nectar itself? And so on. The flute—
It should be understood as being like a dear friend, because it everywhere makes known the state of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s bliss.
The reality characterized by consciousness and bliss is itself the light in the form of the moon, the sun, and so forth.
"With the moon and sun risen together" is an epithet of Vṛndāvana in the two Gautamīya Tantras; that...
And because it is like the eternally full moon, the meaning is that it is both the supreme reality and that which is to be illumined by it.
Likewise, the sense is that it is both the object of relish and the object of enjoyment for them, because it consists of the power of consciousness (cic-chakti).
"He showed his own world to the cowherds, which is beyond darkness" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.28.14); and likewise, in the *Hayaśīrṣa-pañcarātra*, in the description of the reality residing in Vaikuṇṭha:
O Brahmin, listen to the reality of the substance; I shall explain it to you in brief:
there, the trees are wish-fulfilling trees that bestow all enjoyments.
Whatever substance there may be— whether in the form of fragrance, taste, or flowers and the like—
it would possess the nature of flavor and form due to the absence of any portion to be discarded.
"The bark, the seeds, the portions to be discarded, and whatever part is hard—all that you should know to be elemental (bhautika), for it is not composed of the primary elements (bhūtamaya).
Here, the elemental substance would exist in the form of taste and color. Thus [it is said].
The sense is that [the wind] blows from the fragrant [trees] due to being permeated by the sound of your flute and so forth.
"It does not go" means that, through that permeation, those inhabitants do not even perceive time;
or rather, the defects of time do not exist there.
And because of the second verse, "Time is not his prowess," it is for this very reason that Śveta-dvīpa is pure and free from attachment to anything else,
just as a lotus is in a lake.
"He stands indeed upon that ground" (tiṣṭhati tathā-bhūmyāṃ hi tiṣṭhati)—thus from the *Tāpanīya*.
Regarding "the earth" (*kṣiti*), it is said:
"We all do not know him, even though we ask our grandfather" (yaṃ na vidmo vayaṃ sarve pṛcchanto'pi pitāmaham). // 56 //
Then Mahāviṣṇu said to the blessed Prajāpati:
"O Brahman, if your mind is set upon the knowledge of greatness and the creation of progeny,
my child, understand this five-verse lore that I have bestowed."
Thus, having spoken his praise in this manner, he describes the attainment of the grace of the Blessed Lord with the word "atha. Everything is clear. 57.
When the self has awakened through knowledge and devotion, it becomes composed of bliss and consciousness.
Supreme devotion, characterized by love for the Blessed One, arises.
In that regard, he speaks five verses consisting of the nature of serene faith (*prasāda*), beginning with "Prabuddha" [from BhP 11.19.5]:
"Endowed with knowledge and realization, worship Me, being permeated by devotion.
Thus [it is said] from the Eleventh [Book]. (58)
By constantly awakening oneself through the means of valid cognition, the conduct of the virtuous, and their repeated practice,
one shall attain even the highest devotion.
He states the means for attaining the two forms of devotion— namely, that characterized by love and that consisting of the knowledge of the means—
by saying "by the authorities" (*pramāṇaiḥ*). These are the scriptures of the Lord, the conduct of His devotees, and those saintly persons who belong to Him.
Through their conduct, practices, and repeated cultivation of those very things,
he awakens himself by means of his own self; thus, having taken refuge in the Blessed Lord, he personally experiences his own nature as a pure individual soul (*jīva*).
From that, one attains even higher, pure devotion.
And so it is said in the *Śrutistava*:
"In these cities created by oneself, there is a concealment both inside and outside."

"They call you the Supreme Person, a portion manifested by the Holder of All Potencies. Having thus discerned Your human state, the wise, placing their trust in You, worship Your foot—the harvest of the Vedas and the source of non-birth on this earth. (BhP 10.87.20) Thus [ends the verse]. 59.
One should cultivate that very devotion which accomplishes nothing other than me— that devotion for which there is no greater good and by which one attains final liberation.
Abandoning all other doctrines, worship me alone with full confidence;
for whatever the nature of one's faith may be, such will be the accomplishment.
Performing action continuously, this world follows along;
meditating upon Me through that very action, it desires supreme devotion.

Furthermore, strengthening pure devotional practice (*sādhana-bhakti*) itself, [the author] says "other dharmas" to show that one should perform that very practice even without desire for other fruits. As it has been said:
"Whether free from desire, desiring all things, or desiring liberation, the person of noble intellect..."
"One should worship the Supreme Person with intense yoga of devotion" (BhP 2.3.10). Thus [it is said]. 61.
For I am indeed the seed of the entire universe, both moving and non-moving; I am the primary cause, both primordial matter (prakṛti) and the Spirit (puruṣa).
I have bestowed this splendor upon you; O Ordainer, sustain it and likewise protect the worlds.
Therefore, he states with reasoning that even your desire to create will bear fruit: "For I... [and so on]. *Pradhāna* means the most excellent seed;
*prakṛti*, the unmanifest, is the complete form of the Lord.
The person is the seer of that; what need is there for much? You too bear this splendor placed and entrusted by me;
therefore, by means of that...
"O Vidhi, by my splendor, create all the worlds, both moving and unmoving! //62//
Thus ends the commentary named *Digdarśinī*, composed by Śrīla Śrīpāda Śrī Jīva Gosvāmī, on the fifth chapter titled "The Root Sūtras" of the *Śrī Brahma-saṃhitā*.
